author: Musab Alshafie Mohamed
title: Who Speaks for Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms?
content:
When four members of Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms travelled to London in March 2026 to accept the Chatham House Prize on behalf of the movement, the ceremony was widely celebrated as a moment of recognition for one of the most remarkable grassroots humanitarian responses in recent memory. Since fighting broke out between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces in April 2023, ERR volunteers have sustained communal kitchens, health centres, water systems, and evacuation networks across thirteen states, reaching millions of people in areas where international aid organisations simply cannot operate. The Nobel Peace Prize nomination followed. The global attention kept growing.


But inside the movement, a quieter and more difficult question has been building: who actually speaks for Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms, and through what process are those representatives chosen?


I spent the first half of 2026 conducting research on this question for my dissertation at the London School of Economics, interviewing fifteen ERR volunteers and humanitarian practitioners in Arabic. What I found complicates the picture that international audiences have been given.


Emergency Response Room, Kassala, eastern Sudan. Photo credit: Faiz Abubakr.


The Emergency Response Rooms did not build a coordination structure because they wanted one. They built one because the scale of the crisis, and the growing demands of international donors, made it unavoidable. In November 2023, ERRs established the Localisation Coordination Council to manage coordination across state-level networks, engage with national and international humanitarian partners, and create a body that donors could recognise and fund. As one volunteer said: it was “a necessity born of the scale of the crisis, not our original intent.”


The LCC’s founding charter reveals a structural imbalance that has received almost no public attention. Khartoum is allocated seven seats on the Council, one for each of its localities. Every other state in Sudan receives one seat, regardless of population, displacement figures, or the scale of humanitarian need on the ground. Darfur, which has five states and is home to some of the most acute suffering of the entire conflict, has five votes in total. Khartoum has seven. This is not an emergent imbalance that developed over time. It is written into the founding document. It means that Khartoum-based ERRs have disproportionate influence over agenda-setting, donor engagement, and funding priority decisions from the very beginning.


The consequences are visible. Multiple volunteers I spoke to, from states outside Khartoum, described feeling that their priorities were not adequately represented in LCC discussions, and that the decisions most visible to international donors reflected Khartoum’s perspective more than the movement as a whole.


The situation of Women’s Response Rooms makes the problem more acute. These are groups that emerged specifically to address the needs of women and girls during the conflict, providing safe spaces, health services, and psychosocial support in communities where women could not safely access general ERR facilities. The LCC charter recognises Women’s Response Rooms as a designated category of funding support. Money can, in principle, flow to them. But they have no seat on the body that decides how funding priorities are set. They are a recipient category, not a decision-making actor. The result is that Women’s Response Rooms have received only minimal funding allocations, around five per cent, despite clearly articulated needs, while resources are directed toward more generalised priorities like food and water.


This brings us back to London, and to the question that the Chatham House Prize ceremony left unanswered. The four ERR members who accepted the award included volunteers working on gender-responsive support and a co-founder from South Kordofan, a diverse and symbolically significant group. But the LCC’s own charter states explicitly that members must not speak on behalf of the LCC publicly without prior authorisation. No public account has explained how that authorisation was granted, or through which internal process those specific representatives were selected to speak for a movement of more than 20,000 volunteers across thirteen states.


This is not a criticism of the individuals who travelled to London. It is a question about the system. About whether the people who speak for the …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: The “Rape Tournament”: Online Humour and Normalisation of Rape Culture in Namibia
content:
Between April 2024 and February 2025, Namibia recorded

 4,405 cases


of gender-based violence (GBV), of which 1,345 were cases of rape. These figures may not reflect the actual prevalence, as many incidents, particularly in rural communities, remain unreported due to persistent barriers to reporting. The most recent shocking case happened in June when a


25-year-old

 woman was gang raped at knife point by nine minors aged between 15 and 17. The news spread widely across social media, and with it came a violent


discourse

.

 One might expect that such dark and painful news would spark empathy, outrage, and solidarity. Instead, the news was met with many jokes, victim-blaming, sexual objectification, and open mockery of the survivor. These online comments are not merely insensitive humour. It is a disturbing display of how sexual violence is normalised and reveals social evidence of a broader rape culture in Namibia.


When Rape Becomes a “Tournament”


The title of this article emerged

from w

hat unfolded in the Facebook comment sections where the case, in effect, turned into a “rape tournament.”  At the dawn of the news, Namibians on Facebook rephrased this incident from a crime to sports, competition, and masculine camaraderie. In

this

Facebook discourse, the 9 suspects lined up in the photo like a football team, sparking sports references. A significant proportion of users, predominantly male, mocked the incident, curious about who the

“man of the match”

 was and who

“kicked the first penalty”.

 They further referred to the assault as a

“round-robin tournament,”

all of which transformed this violent crime into a public spectacle. 


This discourse appeared to erase the criminal and dehumanising act and reduced the survivor’s trauma to jokes and entertainment. Thus, the “rape tournament” term is used deliberately not to sensationalise the crime, but to describe how many commenters collectively reframed gang rape as though it were a sporting event. These comments construct an entirely different narrative about the survivor and perpetrators. She is no longer portrayed as a survivor of violence. She is rather signified as a playing field upon which the “match” occurred. This, in turn, frames the perpetrators as players whose acts are evaluated, celebrated, and compared. This shows that the football jokes were not isolated comments but formed a pattern.  


The social media comment section acts as a cultural space in which violence is publicly rehearsed, reinforced and legitimised.


The humour masked the true horror of the assault. When rape becomes a tournament, it sustains the rape culture in Namibia. Sexual violence alone does not sustain rape culture; it is also fed by the everyday attitudes, language, and habits that excuse, downplay, or normalise these acts. At its core, these Facebook comments show exactly how humour is used as a tool to keep rape culture alive and well in online spaces.


Victim Blaming Masked as Safety Concerns


Victim-blaming

 rarely appeared in explicit form. It was masked as “safety advice,” in which commenters framed their responses as concern for women’s safety. A significant number of people questioned why she was out that late at night,

with

one male user cautioning all women to stay indoors as soon as the streetlights go on to protect themselves. Women were advised not to walk at night, not to make unnecessary movements after dark

.

 One female commenter even suggested that the survivor should have remained at the home of the man she had allegedly visited and simply endured the “walk of shame” the following morning. At face value, these comments appear protective. However, they subtly relocate responsibility from those who commit violence to those who experience it. The discussion therefore ceases to ask why boys assaulted a woman and instead asks why a woman was outside.


The safety of women in Namibia is a concern given the increasing GBV-related cases in the country. However, the Facebook discussion extended beyond safety concerns and focused predominantly on regulating women’s movements, clothing, relationships and behaviour while remaining largely silent on the conduct of the alleged perpetrators. This kind of talk just aims to control women instead of questioning violent and toxic male behaviour. The burden of preventing sexual violence was therefore relocated from those who commit it to those who experience it. This sheds light on the double standards on …

author: WoMin
title: Wathint’ Abafazi, Wathint’ Imbokodo: Why Challenging Xenophobia Is Unfinished Women’s Business
content:
On 17 August, SADC leaders concluded their 46th summit in Durban, against a backdrop of heightened xenophobic protests, threats, and forced repatriations. August is Women’s Month in South Africa commemorating 70 years since women marched on the Union Buildings fighting against apartheid and pass laws. However, this month has been marred by the recent spate of Afrophobia and xenophobia across the country. SADC’s communiqué recorded an update from South Africa on migration governance and called for coordinated regional dialogue on the drivers of migration. It did not explicitly name xenophobia or Afrophobia — even after months in which Black African migrants have faced intimidation, violence, and pressure to leave South Africa. In an 

Open Letter

 to the SADC Heads of State and Government, WoMin African Alliance, together with The People’s Dialogue, calls for those Heads of State to place xenophobia and Afrophobia in South Africa on its formal agenda, issue a clear public resolution, and commit to measurable regional action. 


Those 20 000 courageous women across race, class and religion marched on 9 August 1956 to confront the Apartheid regime’s institutionalisation of white supremacy and racial capitalism by controlling Black life and movement. The Pass Laws inscribed that control, requiring pass books at all times, and described Black people as “aliens” and “illegal” in the country of their birth. Sophie De Bruyn, the only living leader at this year’s commemoration, shared “that the freedom we marched and bled for is in reality a painful paradox. How can we celebrate our past victories when our current realities are so deeply disappointing and distressful?”  


The pass laws did not simply restrict movement — they dictated who belonged where, who could work, where they could live, and who counted as fully human within South Africa’s borders.  


This historic day of protest was about fighting for a free, democratic South Africa in which all peoples, regardless of race, class and gender, could be emancipated and live with dignity and equality. Already liberated countries on the continent stood alongside Black South Africans in full solidarity, offering a home, bearing the brunt of economic pressure and military assault, especially for frontline states.  


While the pass laws are painful history, the current reality for Black South Africans falls far short of our freedom dreams. Much of Apartheid endures in lived memory — continued spatial injustice, the deepest economic inequality globally, and more than 33.6% unemployment. 


For WoMin African Alliance, rooted in Pan African feminist politics, this is no coincidence. Women’s Month cannot be commemorated as mere nostalgia — it must be treated as unfinished business. The emergence of Xenophobia and Afrophobia results from deep, intersecting crises in South Africa, as set out in our 

statement

 on Afrophobia and Xenophobia. 


The root cause of this crisis is the neoliberal economic policies implemented by the South African government, along with a long history of racial capitalism in which Black people were exploited for cheap labour to build the economy but have remained economically and politically excluded. What we are witnessing is the crumbling and disintegration of our society. Today, South Africa’s huge unemployment rate represents millions of lives suspended in a state of permanent insecurity. This disintegration has the greatest impact and consequences on Black women. 


Impacts on women

 


Women face the most inequality, earning 23% to 35% less than men for the same work, and accounted for 77% of all job losses in 2025. They are concentrated in low-income, informal, or precarious employment such as domestic work. Women-headed households face a roughly 60% chance of being poor. This places a triple burden on women, who bear most unpaid domestic work and child-rearing — labour unrecognised in national accounts and that hampers their economic advancement. 


These statistics represent structural violence rooted in inequality, patriarchy, social dislocation, and dispossession. Rather than confront the state’s failure to transform the economy and property relations, create decent work, or provide basic services, migrants become easy scapegoats for crises produced by capitalist and neoliberal policy. The unemployed South African is encouraged to blame the Zimbabwean street vendor, the Ethiopian spaza shop owner, or the Somali trader, instead of asking why …

author: Wandia Njoya
title: Strange Bedfellows: What’s Faith Got to Do With Identity
content:
What does faith have to do with identity? This is what I asked when I was invited to give a keynote lecture on 18 September 2025 at a workshop held at the Centre for Interfaith Studies in Africa at the Hekima University College in Nairobi. The theme of the workshop was “Law, Education and Interfaith Relations in Kenya”.


I will again begin my reflections with this question: What does faith have to do with identity? My answer today, although I might change my mind later on, is going to be provocative. I think faith has nothing to do with identity. In my presentation, I argue that if we are truly people of faith, the question of identity should not be anywhere near our faith. And I will anchor my argument in the stories of healing in the gospels.


​When I received the invitation to give the lecture, the first story I thought of was that of Jesus with the Samaritan woman at the well, narrated in John 4. 


The passage reveals an extended discussion of identity, in the worldly sense of identity as we know it today. We know identity as exclusion, boundaries, and conflict, rather than as unity, love, and sharing. But remember the political regime of the time of Jesus was the Roman Empire, which the British Empire mimicked when they came here in the late 1800s, and then left another mimicry called independence. We are therefore living under a mimicry of the same Roman Empire under which Jesus lived. 


The political logic that runs the Euro-American global empire, now in decline, was revived in Europe in the 17

th

 century from the ruins of the Roman Empire in a process that was baptized the Renaissance. As far as I’m concerned, there was no renaissance. It was a festival of exploring and excavating graves, in the same way the colonialists did when they came to Africa in the early 1900s, and still do, in the name of verifying whether we were “civilized”. The Roman Empire died in 476 of the Common Era, but when the wealthy of Europe, like the Medici family, wanted to impress the rest of Italy and Europe, they hired artists and scientists to excavate the graves and monuments of the dead empire and seek inspiration for something new. They essentially looked for the living among the dead. So, ideas such as the state, senate, law, and even the management of people of multiple cultural backgrounds, were borrowed from the ruins of Rome.  


Rome operated as a centralized government with a multicultural mix of people from the peripheral provinces of the empire. Not all people of the empire were considered Romans or citizens. Historians mark the reign of Augustus as the point at which citizenship transformed from being an active one about rights and duties, to a passive one about legal status and honour. Under Augustus, the Latin language gained more prominence as a marker of “Romanness”, and the empire continued to make a distinction between those who were born in Rome and those who were not. Later on, as Rome began to decline, it invited the Barbarians, whom they considered the Germanic peoples to be, to fight for the Roman empire while simultaneously not accessing the rights of citizens of Rome.


The Romans named “Barbarians” those whom they considered to be outsiders to the empire, those whose languages were incomprehensible to them.

While Western epistemology has since clarified that the Germanic, Slavic, Croat, Turkish, and other Europeans were those to whom the Romans attached the tag “Barbarian”, it has not done equal favour to North Africa, where “Berbers” and “Arabs” are still ethnically tied to the imperial term. Meanwhile, the expression “barbarians at the gate” became a popular one to capture the fear of the insiders that their city was facing imminent collapse at the hands of immigrants.


Back to John 4. As we see in his conversation with the Samaritan woman, Jesus, who had lived in that same Roman Empire, rejected this imperial view of identity, where discrimination is unspoken yet real when it comes to human interactions. When he asks for water, he’s speaking as one human being to another. But what does the Samaritan woman say? To paraphrase her, she says: “According to my ethnicity, I’m not worthy to give you water.” Then Jesus replies, “But the water I’m providing is of eternal life, meaning that even when I ask you for literal water, I reject this imperial idea of human hierarchy.”


Then Jesus tests her with another identity, which is that of gender. He asks her for a husband, and then reveals that he …

author: Hassan Alnaser, Mohamed Alagra, Mashair Idris
title: Sudan Nashra: Military strikes RSF convoy inside Chadian territory, sparks regional concerns | Kauda fighting pushes Otoro groups to demand Hilu’s removal from SPLM-N leadership | US proposes nationwide arms embargo on Sudan in Security Council
content:
Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter

here

.


Washington is pushing in the United Nations Security Council to take the Darfur arms embargo nationwide.


US Senior Advisor on Arab and African Affairs Massad Boulos put the proposal on the table on Monday, after first floating the idea at a council session in June. The draft would expand the 2005 Darfur sanctions regime to all of Sudan, while explicitly bringing drones and related technology under the embargo. The current regime expires in September unless amended or renewed.


Boulos pointed to the growing toll from drone warfare, saying drones accounted for nearly 80 percent of casualties this year and that both sides continue to strike civilians and civilian infrastructure.


Khartoum rejected the proposal outright. Sudan’s ambassador to the UN Al-Harith Idriss said applying the same restrictions nationwide would amount to equating “the state institutions and the rebel militia,” calling the proposal an attack on Sudan’s sovereignty.


Washington has to get past Russia and China, which both pushed back against expanding the sanctions regime and can veto any council resolution. So while the proposal has support from some council members, it is unlikely to go anywhere without a compromise.


Sudan’s drone war crossed its borders twice over the past days.


In western Sudan, military drones struck a convoy of hundreds of Rapid Support Forces vehicles on August 20 inside Chad’s eastern Ennedi region, near the Sudanese border. Two Sudanese military sources said the convoy had been assembled over several weeks at camps in southeastern Libya, and was preparing to enter Darfur through Chad using a new route through North Darfur’s Wadi Howar.


Chad condemned the strike as a violation of its sovereignty and warned that it reserved the right to respond, prompting the African Union to call for restraint and dialogue to prevent a regional escalation. The Sudanese military has yet to comment. 


On the other side of the country, the military said a strategic drone crossed into Blue Nile State from Ethiopian territory and was shot down over Dindro. 


Inside the RSF camp, its main ally in the war and its parallel government, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North, led by Abdel Aziz al-Hilu, continues to grapple with an internal crisis that is becoming harder to contain.


Fighting with one of its oldest constituencies, the Otoro tribe, has returned to Kauda, the movement’s political and military center in South Kordofan, with control shifting between the two sides over the past two weeks.


RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo intervened and called for a ceasefire, but overlapping control on the ground made that impossible to sustain. The ceasefire collapsed, and Otoro fighters regained the upper hand in Kauda.


Some Otoro groups are now calling for Hilu to step down and are seeking alliances with other Nuba Mountains constituencies to challenge a political order that the SPLM-N has dominated for decades, but which has increasingly been concentrated in a narrow circle around Hilu, two Otoro leaders told Mada Masr.


And while there is still no end in sight to the war’s battles, Khartoum is preparing to use September’s UN General Assembly in New York to consolidate a post-Khartoum political posture and present its vision for Sudan’s political and institutional order after the war, according to Sudanese diplomatic and government sources informed of the preparations. 


Transitional Sovereignty Council Chair Abdel Fattah al-Burhan remains the leading option to head the delegation. But US sanctions imposed on him in 2025 could make his participation complicated, prompting the government to consider other senior officials if necessary.


The government plans to put its internal political dialogue on the New York agenda. The process, now being hurried in Khartoum, is to be presented as nationally owned, with international actors there to support and facilitate rather than dictate its agenda or outcome.


But a political source close to the dialogue said New York will test the international response to a process whose current, state-curated form is already being rejected by parts of the civilian political camp. 


Sudanese political and civilian forces, opposed to both the war and a military-led political process, rejected Burhan’s call for a dialogue, saying that any process launched while fighting continues — and conducted under military control — would reproduce …

author: ROAPE
title: The murder of Professor Jason Arday
content:
On Sunday 16 August I joined the vigil for Professor Arday in London’s Trafalgar Square in the summer’s heat, packed tight with thousands of protestors marking their respect, holding bunches of flowers aloft, and placards reading, ‘Rest in Power Professor Jason Arday.’ Heads bowed, hundreds around me in tears – the words of his students unbearable, our anger craving a response. 


Professor Arday is dead. Murdered. Yet again another Black person has been killed – pilloried in a public execution orchestrated by a profoundly racist press, and organised fascists.


The vigil spoke to the structural racism that shaped Professor Arday’s life and death. I was struck by British MP Diane Abbott’s comments on the Black experience in the UK and the racism encountered daily. This daily experience is engrained in British institutions, the press and political life.


His family commented about the outpouring of grief and fury, describing their emotions: ‘The public cruelty Jason was subjected to was too much for any man to bear. The outpouring of love, support, and grief since his death means so much to us. Although it is bittersweet now, kindness is needed in life, not just in death.’


Bittersweet indeed – the kindness, support and grief were essential but too late. 


Professor Jason Arday – the Black professor of sociology at Cambridge University – was hounded to his death by a racist campaign to unseat him from his position. In the 22 days leading to his suicide, there were 249 articles in major newspapers in the UK, continual coverage on TV, radio and blogs. This had followed a repeated effort to undermine Arday since he became a professor at the university in 2023.


The noise from this pogrom – accusing him of plagiarism, lies, bombast, academic fakery – was overwhelming. Many people who should have known better joined the chorus. The UK’s mainstream liberal paper, 

The Guardian,

 

launched an investigation into Arday’s scholarship

. I encountered family members who joined in the chorus – denouncing Arday, ridiculing his claims, and his work.


On 5 August, Arday resigned from his post; the following week, on 14 August, he committed suicide. A man described by his students as ‘gentle’, ‘caring’, ‘compassionate’ and ‘inspiring’ was systematically broken – destroyed in a campaign which led directly to his suicide. 


Arday was murdered. 


This was the objective – Arday’s suicide was the logical outcome. Leading the recent crusade was the racist scholar, Nathan Cofnas, who published on his Substack the blog, ‘

DEI Fraud and Cover-Up at Cambridge

’, on 21 July 2026.  A vile man who targeted and conducted his own investigation into Arday’s work  – charging him with plagiarism, which confirmed Cofnas’ thesis that Black people are inferior, unworthy of senior academic positions. 


Cofnas is a symptom of our times. A marginal, bigoted voice that once would have remained largely undetected in the swamp is now amplified by a mainstream, racist agenda. In the global North, these voices have reached fever pitch – finding traction in a political climate that has seen right-wing governments elected, and racist policies normalised in daily political speech. 


To say these developments are worrying is a grotesque understatement – these are clarion signs of our current and deepening crisis, and the irredeemable racism of our political and economic system. This cannot be absorbed and understood simply as a British thing. We see the same tightening of the screw in the personal attacks on International Criminal Court judges and the normalisation of genocide.


There are three observations that I want to make in this piece. Firstly, I want to look at two political parallels –  one that prompted the global mass movement, Black Lives Matter, a few years ago, and the second when antisemitism was denounced by the French author Émile Zola at the end of the 19

th

 century. Finally, I want to say a few things about plagiarism and academia. 


On 25 May 2020 in Minneapolis, George Floyd was stopped by the police, then wrestled to the ground by police officer Derek Chauvin – clips of his slow death over nine minutes were beamed across the planet. Chauvin was later convicted of murder. George Floyd was choked to death by Chauvin, who pinned Floyd to the ground, as he died – filmed by the incredibly brave 17-year-old Darnella Frazie – he was heard saying,‘Mama, mama, mama’, ‘Momma, I love you,’ and ‘Momma! I’m through.’


George Floyd was …

author: Simon Ramapuputla
title: Marikana’s wounds still bleed 14 years after police massacre
content:
Fourteen years after police opened fire on striking mineworkers at Marikana, the massacre is remembered not only for the 34 men who were killed, but for their absence in the lives of their families.


For some, the memory is of a father who never came home. For others, it is the loss of a breadwinner, a brother or a son. And for those who were children when the killings happened, it is the experience of growing up with memories that have become increasingly distant, while the questions about justice remain.


At a commemoration marking 14 years since the massacre, the families, activists and academics reflected on what Marikana means more than a decade later – and on its place in South Africa’s longer history of protest, police violence and struggles for dignity.


For the Socio-Economic Rights Institute of South Africa (Seri), which has represented the families since 2012, the central question remains accountability. Seri secured payments for 35 of the 37 families whose loved ones were killed by police. Two families have received no compensation.


Seri’s executive director, Nomzamo Zondo said the compensation process itself reflected a deeper problem in how the state understood the loss suffered by the families. “Part of that is a narrative that what the state is interested in compensating is the income that the miners would have earned. They do not want to account for the husbands, brothers, sons and fathers that they took away from the families,” she said.


For Zondo, compensation alone cannot address the significance of Marikana. The state also needs to acknowledge that the massacre should never have happened, she argued: “That’s what a public holiday on the 16

th

 of August would mean. It would say: we are saying never, never again.”


She said this was particularly important given the continued use of force by police in managing protests. “We’ve seen that police continue to manage protests through the use of violence. They have continuously refused to accept that their role is to facilitate protests as a constitutional right.”


Zondo also pointed to the failure to implement recommendations made by the panel of experts on public order policing and the management of protests. The panel completed its work in 2018, but its recommendations remain largely unimplemented.


Squalid living conditions in the informal settlement, Nkaneng, in the shadow of Marikana platinum mine, a source of immense wealth for the owners in 2012, Lonmin. Archive photo by The Benchmarks Foundation


Another major concern, she said, was the failure of the National Prosecuting Authority to bring those responsible for the 16 August killings to court. “Every year, of course, when the anniversary comes, there is an explanation that work is being done,” Zondo said. “But now we are like one year short from 15 years since the massacre. We are just 12 years since the Commission finalised its report and recommended that the NPA must investigate and charge whoever is responsible.”


The question, she said, was whether there was “really an intention to hold anyone accountable for the deaths of the 16

th

 of August”.


For the families, however, the consequences of Marikana are not measured only by the progress of criminal investigations or compensation claims. They are lived in the absence of loved ones.


‘I still have that memory’


NowilI Nungu was 15 when her father, Jackson Lehopa, was killed at Marikana. Today, at 29, she remembers him through the ordinary moments of their life together: travelling to school on a bicycle, buying him a Coke and watching him repair the bicycle whenever it broke.


“I have so many memories with my dad,” Nungu said. She was the only girl among six children and had been living with her father in Rustenburg while her mother moved back to the Eastern Cape.


By the time of the massacre, Nungu had moved to the Eastern Cape with her mother. The family did not have electricity and relied on the radio for news. Her father normally called every day after returning from the koppie to tell them he was safe. But that day, he did not call.


Crosses erected at the koppie as a symbol of lives lost on 16 August 2012. Archive photo by Muzi Mzoyi


Sebolai Liau lost his father, the late Janefeke Raphael Liau, at Marikana. For him, the question of justice remains unresolved. “I think regarding the Marikana massacre, there is no justice. I don’t think it will ever be served, but for now it has not been, and there are no signs …

author: Tsion Gurmu - Nekessa Opoti - Jason Mosebach
title: No Place to Call Home: Increasing Homophobic & Transphobic Laws in the U.S. & Africa
content:
A network of Christian evangelical organizations has spent nearly two decades and tens of millions of dollars fueling

a storm of anti-LGBTI+ legislation across Africa

.

 That same network now drafts and bankrolls a parallel wave of anti-LGBTI legislation including anti-trans bills

sweeping through American statehouses

.

 Meanwhile, new and expanding U.S. immigration laws increasingly restrict access to refuge for endangered migrants and regularly return those who found safety back to the danger they fled. Together, these trends form a closed circuit of violence and oppression that prevents Black LGBTI+ migrants from finding safety, community, and home on either side of the Atlantic. 

 


Africa’s Widening Net

 


In recent years, many African countries have criminalized same-sex relations for the first time; several others have revived dormant colonial-era statutes or expanded upon

existing anti-LGBTI+ laws

.

 Today, thirty-three African countries

criminalize homosexuality

.

 This rise is sharpest in West Africa: Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger have each criminalized same-sex relations for the first time and, along with Senegal and Ghana, which now criminalize even the 

“promotion” of LGBTI+ identity

.


By contrast, non-criminalizing countries cluster most heavily in

Southern Africa

,

 home Namibia and Botswana, which, in the last two years, became the only two African countries to repeal their

anti-LGBTI+ laws

.

 It’s also home to South Africa, the country with the continent’s most meaningful LGBTI+ protections. Its Constitution explicitly bars discrimination based on sexual orientation, and a 2024 hate-crimes law also added formal protections for gender identity.

 Even there, stigma and harm persist, as hate crimes disproportionately target Black LGBTI+ South Africans.


Uganda’s 2023 “Anti-Homosexuality Act” serves as a template for other nations building or expanding their own anti-LGBTI+ regimes, and it did not emerge from Ugandan politics alone. Several American evangelical groups spent years laying its groundwork: hosting conferences in Kampala, addressing Uganda’s Parliament directly, and framing LGBTI+ identity as a foreign threat to “

family values

.”

 The result is one of the world’s most severe anti-LGBTI+ regimes, imposing life imprisonment for same-sex activity; the death penalty for “aggravated homosexuality”; and up to

twenty years imprisonment for supporting LGBTI+ people and organizations

.

 This template of oppression has already found imitators. 

Kenya’s pending “Family Protection Bill” borrows its death penalty language directly and imposes a comparable ten-year minimum sentence

for promoting LGBTI+ rights

.

 Ghana’s “Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill” introduces a similar promotion ban and a duty to report LGBTI+ activity, encouraging citizens

to surveil and denounce one another

.

 In Senegal, 

a member of the ruling party declared that “Homosexuals will no longer breathe in [Senegal]” as parliament passed a

law

 doubling the prison sentence for same-sex relations and criminalizing LGBTI+ advocacy and “transsexuality”—extending the law beyond conduct to gender expression itself.

 


None of this is incidental. The same evangelical network funding Uganda’s law is at work elsewhere, spreading anti-LGBTI+ rhetoric and influence far beyond Uganda’s borders.

 It is one coordinated campaign of hate, not thirty-three separate national stories.

 


America’s Parallel Turn

 


The U.S. is writing its own version of this same story of hate and exclusion. State legislatures introduced more than 600 anti-LGBTI+ bills in 2025 alone, up from roughly 500 

in 2024

.

 At least seventy are now law, and twenty-nine states have adopted at least one of four common restrictions: limits on gender-affirming care, bans on transgender athletes, bathroom laws, or rules against using a person’s chosen name or pronouns.


A new wave of anti-LGBTI+ legislation—so called “sex-definition” statutes—goes further still, fixing a person’s legal sex at birth and applying that definition across all of state government, reaching far beyond earlier laws’ narrower targets. For example: Kansas’s S.B. 244 invalidates and reissues any driver’s license or birth certificate that doesn’t match a person’s sex at birth, mandates that public bathrooms be sex-segregated, and writes a single biological definition of sex into every

Kansas statute

.

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Recentering African Feminist Epistemologies: A Community of Practice to Prevent and Respond to Sexual Violence
content:
Over the past year, Liberation Alliance Africa has sustained the

Building Knowledge Bridges Community of Practice on Recentering African Indigenous Epistemologies to Prevent and Respond to Sexual Violence

. This Community of Practice is a collective of African feminist scholars, practitioners, organisers, artists, and movement builders committed to the dreaming and making of a world free from sexual violence through knowledge bridges.


Sexual violence continues to impact communities across the African continent, and class, ethnicity and religion play a critical role in making civilians in conflict-affected countries particularly more vulnerable. It disproportionately affects women and girls, and ethnic, gender and racialized minorities. Sexual violence is compounded by conflict, displacement, poverty, and gender inequality. It remains significantly under-reported due to stigma and under-prosecuted? Due to weak and corrupt justice systems. Sexual violence includes rape and sexual assault, sexual coercion and exploitation, including trafficking for sexual exploitation and conflict-related sexual violence such as using rape as a weapon of war. It affects people of any gender and age. 


Our starting premise is simple: sexual violence on the continent cannot be understood, let alone addressed, through frameworks that treat colonialism as history rather than a structural force that continues to shape theory, practice, and response to sexual violence. 


Coloniality was

coined

by Peruvian philosopher and sociologist Aníbal Quijano, and it describes the long-lasting pattern of power produced by colonial rule and shape

s

 how we approach epistemological frameworks through which violence is understood.

Epistemology deals with questions concerning the nature, scope, and sources of knowledge.

 A meaningful analysis of sexual violence must begin by seeking to decolonise knowledge and epistemic structures. This analysis requires us to interrogate the assumptions that underpin dominant theories, question whose expertise is legitimised, and create space for African feminist epistemologies to shape how violence is understood, prevented, and responded to. 


We felt an urgent need to organise as scholars and practitioners to generate new frameworks grounded in our histories, political realities, and lived experiences. Our analyses are rooted in our confrontation of the neo-colonial state, the global imperialist, extractive and patriarchal systems that shape our everyday existence. We arrive as feminists in service of a liberatory project, convinced that knowledge-making is itself a site of feminist struggle. 


As the CoP came together through both intentional convening and organic growth, we began organising our work around three enquiries that we believe are critical to envisioning a decolonial feminist approach to preventing and responding to sexual violence in Africa. 


The first enquiry,

Whose Knowledge? An Audit of the Current Knowledge Systems within Sexual Violence Prevention and Response in Africa

 examines the dominant literature, asks whose voices have shaped the field, whose knowledge has been marginalised, and what becomes possible when African feminist scholarship is placed at the centre of analysis. 


The second enquiry,

 The Coloniality of Sexual Violence: Gender, Power, Sovereignty, and the Neo-Colonial State,

 advances interventions on sexual violence that explicitly interrogate the role and impact of hetero-patriarchal colonial racial-capitalism, alongside the complicity of neo-colonial states, in producing and sustaining conditions of gendered violence. 


The third enquiry,

Truth-telling and Epistemic Sovereignty in the Prevention and Response Continuum

, centres on indigenous and endogenous knowledge systems as essential practice-based frameworks for reimagining prevention, response, healing, accountability, and collective safety.


The Imperative of Recentering African Epistemologies


At Liberation Alliance Africa, we believe African women and gender-expansive people’s knowledge-making and world-building are crucial to de-westernising normative assumptions and dominant approaches. African women and gender-expansive scholars must nurture new ways of knowing and being- knowledge that doesn’t just challenge dominant views, but creates a rich foundation for how we understand reality and tackle life’s critical questions.

author: WoMin
title: On Language and the Pedagogy of Liberation
content:
Across Africa, colonialism was not only a project of economic exploitation and political domination; it was also a project of language and cultural control. Colonial rule sought to determine not only who governed and who had access to resources but also elevated European languages as symbols of intelligence and authority, while African languages were systematically marginalised. 


African literature captured this contradiction. In

So Long a Letter

, Mariama Bâ writes from within the tensions of expressing African women’s realities through a language inherited from colonial rule. Ama Ata Aidoo’s novel

Our Sister Killjoy

, similarly, exposes the uneasy relationship between English as a language of literary expression and also as a reminder of cultural displacement. These reflections continue to resonate with present-day realities across the continent, where language remains deeply entangled with questions of power, culture, identity, class, gender, and belonging.  


Today, access to education, legal systems, government services, and political participation in many African countries still depends heavily on competence in colonial languages such as English, French, or Portuguese.  


In Nigeria, for example, although more than 250 languages are spoken across the country, English remains the dominant language of governance, education or even policy discourse. Similar dynamics persist elsewhere on the continent. In Tanzania, although Kiswahili is the national language, many court judgments continue to be delivered in English. Citizens who do not understand English must depend on interpreters to comprehend legal decisions affecting their lives. 


For peasant and working-class women confronting mining, oil extraction, logging, large-scale agricultural investments, and other extractive projects, language exclusions carry profound consequences especially for rural women whose language is deeply tied to their relationship to land, water, forests, food systems, ancestry, and survival.  


Where information about government-proposed projects is often delivered in foreign languages without clarifying their implications including the terms of the proposed project, the risks it poses, the compensation being offered, or the legal mechanisms available to challenge it, their ability to give meaningful consent or organise resistance against it, then language becomes a question of power. 


Language in Women Learning Liberation and Translation as a Tool of Resistance

 


Language was central to the development of

Women Learning Liberation

  (WLL), WoMin’s 18-month political education course for frontline women activists. The first WLL cohort began in July 2024, bringing together 60 women from Cameroon, Guinea Conakry, Ivory Coast, Madagascar, South Africa, and Uganda. From the beginning, WLL understood political education not as the transfer of knowledge from experts to communities, but as a process of collective learning rooted in women’s own experiences and struggles. 


The Ugandan WLL cohort spoke eight languages and represented five different community struggles. English could provide a common language for some discussions, but relying exclusively on it would have risked excluding women from fully expressing their experiences, questions, analysis, and political imagination. WLL therefore deliberately incorporated interpretation into the political education process. Facilitation moved between English, Luganda, Runyoro, and Kinyarwanda, while participants themselves became active in ensuring that interpretation was taking place. 


As

Ugandan facilitator Sostine Namanya

 explained: “Language can work, but language needs to be budgeted for, language needs to be prepped for.” 


In many African contexts, people come from diverse language backgrounds and often speak multiple languages. While English or French may serve as common languages, reliance on colonial languages can reproduce unequal power relations and weaken movements. Interpretation and translation therefore become powerful tools for building multilingual and robust movements capable of deepening collective participation.  


In 2024, WoMin launched materials supporting the

Right To Say NO  campaign in East Africa

 in five languages, which join a plethora of knowledge materials and resources such as its award-winning film,

Women Hold up the Sky

 (2021) and a comic book,

Voices against Extractivism: Sheroes for Change

author: The Elephant
title: Occupy: Pulpit Kwa Street
content:
Since the “Occupy Churches” mobilisations of 2024, religious institutions across Kenya have come under intensified public scrutiny, not merely over doctrine, but over power, money, and accountability. Citizens are increasingly aware of how certain churches and ministries operate as extractive structures, deploying fear, guilt, miracle-economy promises, and prophetic endorsements to secure tithes, offerings, votes, and social control, while doing far less to advance justice, transparency, social protection, and the common good.


Captain Ibrahim Traoré’s recent interventions in Burkina Faso, in which he has openly questioned how religion should function within a secular republic and cautioned against its use to divide citizens, crystallise a broader continental mood. The issue is not whether religion should disappear from public life, but whether its immense symbolic authority and organisational capacity will serve elite interests or public ethics. Put differently: will churches, mosques, and other religious communities deepen democratic culture and social responsibility, or reinforce patronage, impunity, and sectarianism?


For a younger generation in particular, cynicism about institutional religion has moved beyond the familiar woke labels of the 2010s. Rather, they find it difficult to relate to a religion that has nothing to say about their lived realities. Instead, as a Nation TV news feature covered in 2025, religion has become removed from the daily lives of the people and exists only to endorse the colonial state and the venal class that supports it. What we have is a generation that has rejected the Ideology of Order that religion subjects them to, choosing to leave institutional religion and to define faith on their own terms. For a clergy trained in colonial theology, these phenomena find them in a stalemate. This series therefore explores these tensions. 


As Wandia Njoya notes, faith has nothing to do with identity, and the attempt to include a metaphysical construct to codify racial, gender, and ethnic categories is a Eurocentric lens that only serves to cement division and colonial hierarchies. Elsewhere, Nelly Madegwa and Akal Mohan grapple with their faith in light of a country that desperately needs a prophetic voice to speak to the plight of young people. Finally, Ivan Muyabi, Nyambura Mundia, and Ochillo Oyugi reflect on the failure of the church to create a broader social vision to inspire a younger generation to think about the place of the church in present-day Kenya. Their analysis assembles a portrait that is at once grim and biting, exposing the profound intellectual and moral bankruptcy at the heart of religious life. Confronting this truth is the first step in thinking about the role of religion in society.

author: Hassan Alnaser, Kidus Lemma
title: Once bitter enemies Amhara, Tigray reach understandings in fight against Ethiopian govt
content:
In mid-August, the leader of the Amhara insurgency fighting to overthrow Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed made a surprising announcement. 


The collection of armed Amhara movements fighting in the country’s northwest under the unified Fano umbrella would join an alliance of seven other anti-government groups across the country, Fano leader Zemene Kassie

told

 the Swiss publication, Le Temps.

 


What makes the move surprising is that the alliance includes members of the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), whom the Amhara forces that make up the Fano fought against during the 2020-2022 war.


In addition to the TPLF, the alliance includes forces from Gumuz, Oromo, the Berta people and Somalia, Zemene said. 


At the national level, the fight between Ethiopian oppositional groups and the government comes against the backdrop of a struggle over the future of the country’s multinational federal system and state’s right to self-determination. 


However, this tension has a larger regional dynamic given Ethiopia’s involvement in the war in Sudan and its expressed desire to secure access to the Red Sea either by diplomatic coup or by force. 


While fighting between the Fano and the Ethiopian government has transformed much of the Amhara Region into an active war zone since late 2023, the beginning of August saw clashes between TPLF forces and the Ethiopian military that threatened to transform long standing simmering tensions between the groups into an active war. 


An African Union diplomat based in Addis Ababa told

Mada Masr

 at the time that any expansion of the fighting in Tigray would have an impact on the calculations of every regional actor because the borders linking Sudan, Ethiopia and Eritrea are no longer merely dividing lines between states.

 They now form part of an interconnected regional security system in which domestic wars and geopolitical interests overlap, the diplomat added, making any new outbreak of fighting in Tigray a potential factor in reshaping the security landscape of the entire East African region.


The government has responded to the early August clashes with increased military activity. 


In a statement issued on Friday, the Tigray regional government

warned

the international community that the region is nearing “another catastrophic war.”

 


An economic and security blockade has escalated following clashes that broke out on August 1, the statement added, with air strikes and artillery shelling hitting civilian areas, causing casualties and destruction and disrupting cultural activities.


In an interview with Oromia Broadcasting Network on August 7, Abiy criticized the TPLF leadership, accusing it of clinging to outdated political methods and forging alliances that he said threaten stability. 


TPLF deputy chair Amanuel Assefa pointed to a strike on August 20, when a drone

hit

a residential area in Mekelle, Tigray’s capital.

 Residents speaking to Mada Masr confirmed the strike and said several homes were damaged.


Medical sources at Mekelle’s Ayder Specialized Hospital said 13 people were brought in with injuries following the strike, including five women and children, with three in serious condition. The injured ranged in age from two to 60, the sources said.


Tigrayan authorities also said a second strike hit near Mekelle University, though there is no confirmed information on casualties or damage as of the time of publishing.


The strike on Mekelle came only days after another attack that Tigrayan authorities attributed to the Ethiopian military, where a drone struck a farmers’ training center in the Dandera village, about 15 km from Mekelle, on August 18.


Site of drone strike in Mekelle, Tigray’s capital. August 20. Source: Tigray Communications Affairs Bureau via Facebook


While the government hit Tigray, Fano forces continued to secure strategic wins against the Ethiopian military. 


Fano forces in the Wollo provinces of Amhara – which borders southern Tigray — have

claimed

 significant military victories in the past week along the Raya and Ambasel fronts, capturing strategic cities, highway corridors and key positions beyond the Awash River.

 


Fano forces seized the cities of Robit and Aradum and moved within three km of the city of Kobo. Fano troops also took control of the main Waja-Kobo asphalt highway, a critical transit corridor leading to Addis Ababa. 


And on the Ambasel front, Fano forces ambushed government troops moving from Wuchale …

author: Sara Connors
title: Yukon wildfire agency wants to know why it didn’t get called to B.C.
content:
Yukon First Nations Wildfire is questioning why international crews were deployed to help with wildfires in British Columbia this summer while its own resources remained available – a situation it says has left it feeling sidelined.


As particularly intense wildfires

burned across southern B.C.

 in late July into August, international firefighting crews from as far away as Australia, New Zealand and Mexico were called in to help.


But

Yukon First Nations Wildfire (YFNW)

 says its crews didn’t receive the same opportunity.


“Everybody trains all summer to be able to go out on these deployments, and then they aren’t allowed to when the when the time comes. It makes them feel less than or unequal to,” YFNW CEO Nick Mauro told APTN News. “It is really frustrating.”


Mauro said that for the past five years, its crews have been deployed outside the territory through the Yukon government, with the

Canadian Interagency Forest Fire Centre (CIFFC)

 coordinating the sharing of wildfire resources between provinces and territories.


But he said this year YFNW hasn’t had any deployments through the territorial government.


“(It’s) really frustrating when you have international crews flying in from other continents, and we’re being told that there’s not enough money to drive our crews from the Yukon down south,” he said.


Nick Mauro is the CEO of Yukon First Nations Wildfire. Photo: Jordan Haslbeck/APTN News


A private contractor owned by First Nations development corporations, YFNW offers Type 2-certified firefighting crews, which are trained to support a variety of lower-risk wildfire operations and are employed through contract companies.


They differ from Type 1 crews, which have the highest level of training and are employed directly by provincial or territorial wildfire services.


Sarah Buss, a fire information officer with BC Wildfire Service, said in an email to APTN News that while it recognizes the important role Indigenous crews play in wildfire response, because YFNW is located outside of the province, it would have to be deployed through the Yukon government, with CIFFC coordinating that request.


Meanwhile, Mike Fancie, a spokesperson with Yukon Wildland Fire Management, said that a request first has to come through another jurisdiction, and that B.C. hasn’t requested the type of crew that YFNW provides.


He also noted that the territory can’t force other provinces and territories to accept a resource’s offer to help.


“We are always glad to work with YFNW to support our shared goal of helping people in their time of need, but we cannot promise them fireline opportunities on behalf of other jurisdictions,” he said.


The situation isn’t a surprise to Arnold Lazare, interim CEO with the

National Indigenous Fire Safety Council

, which aims to support Indigenous fire safety programs and capacity.


“There is definitely a disconnect when it comes to the resources being allocated to Indigenous communities,” he said.


He said interjurisdictional barriers involving issues like workers’ compensation and safety, as well as the lack of an accredited national training program, can impact the ability of Indigenous wildfire crews to be deployed.


“That’s where things start getting mixed up,” he said.


He argued that governments could reduce their dependence on foreign firefighters by investing more into Indigenous fire crews closer to home.


He said the council is hoping to create a nationally accredited training program that could be used as a Canada-wide resource, making it easier to deploy Indigenous wildfire crews when and where they’re needed.


Mauro said while he understands the current system wasn’t designed to prioritize the types of resources


YFNW provides, he believes it doesn’t have to stay that way.


He said he’s optimistic there will eventually be systemic changes that will allow local Indigenous wildfire crews like YFNW the right of first refusal before international resources are deployed.


“We want to see the same and equal opportunity for Indigenous crews across Canada, that’s really what matters most to us,” he said. “I’m really hoping that as we continue, there are those in positions of power that are able to help us out.”


A spokesperson for CIFFC said in a statement its working with Indigenous partners to better understand and address barriers to deploying Indigenous wildfire resources.

author: Chris Walker
title: Trump Confidante Laura Loomer Goes on Racist, Islamophobic Tirade Over Weekend
content:
Loomer targeted Florida Senate Democratic nominee Angie Nixon, Ketanji Brown Jackson, and Zeteo‘s Mehdi Hasan, among others.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

This past weekend, far right activist Laura Loomer, an informal adviser to President Donald Trump, made a series of posts on X targeting Democratic lawmakers and candidates for office, as well as progressive media personalities, using racist and Islamophobic terms.

In one post, Loomer tagged Florida Senate candidate Angie Nixon (D), Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minnesota), Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Massachusetts), and Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, claiming that her past criticisms of these individuals were wrongly labeled as racist. But even in that post, Loomer couldn’t resist describing those individuals using racist terms.

“These women are all ghetto, entitled, race-obsessed, destructive black BITCHES who are completely unfit for the power they hold,” Loomer wrote in her post.

Nixon responded to Loomer’s post, calling out some of her antics on social media — including a time in 2024 when the right-wing provocateur ate dog food during a live stream. Afterward, Loomer again reiterated her racist views against Nixon, and derided her for “speak[ing] Ebonics.”

“Maybe I need to bark at you and tug your leash and then you’ll finally understand,” Loomer added.

Nixon defiantly replied to Loomer’s posts. “When referring to me, it’s Representative Angie Nixon. However, after November 3rd, YOU CAN CALL ME SENATOR!” she wrote.

Gov. Wes Moore (D-Maryland) similarly called out Loomer’s racist messages.

“You attack and insult Black women because you believe peddling racism is good for your clicks and your business model. And while everyone with internet access and ignorant opinions doesn’t deserve a response, this is someone who is an advisor of Donald Trump and who should be condemned by all,” Moore said.

Loomer also attacked Zeteo editor-in-chief and founder Mehdi Hasan, asking when he’ll have his citizenship rights “denaturalized” over comments he made in early 2025.

“How can this Islamic invader be allowed to stay in our country when he’s not from here and he tweeted ‘Make American Planes Crash Again’?” Loomer wrote on Saturday, adding, “He should be deported immediately.”

Notably, Hasan’s original statement wasn’t calling for violence against anyone, but rather was a remark in response to a spate of plane crashes in the wake of controversial aviation-related decisions made by the Trump administration.

As Hasan explained in February last year:

I deleted this sarcastic quote-tweet because MAGA and Islamophobic folks are clipping it out of context and trying to ridiculously suggest I’m inciting violence. I was obviously mocking the MAGA slogan…and highlighting the shocking number of plane crashes under Trump and the FAA cuts.

Hasan also responded to Loomer’s comments from this weekend, pointing out a double standard in U.S. political news reporting.

“Serious question to every mainstream news network and newspaper in this country: how can you justify crazy obsessive coverage of Hasan Piker and just totally ignore much worse stuff like this from an actual presidential adviser?” the Zeteo founder wrote.

Loomer’s Islamophobic comments targeted Muslims in general, too, including her expressing a desire to set up an illegal surveillance state system against Muslim Americans.

“I want a Flock Camera outside of every mosque in America,” she wrote.

Loomer isn’t an official member of the Trump administration. However, she has advised the president on numerous matters, primarily relating to hirings and firings during his second term in office.

Most notably, she appeared to play a significant role in the firing of six members of the National Security Council last year. Trump denied Loomer’s influence, but according to reporting at the time, the firings were based in part on a list of people Loomer told Trump would be disloyal to him.

As Trump cracks down on political speech, independent media is increasingly necessary.

author: Dominique Gené - Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Tasiujaq crowd calls for more as Nitjautik Music Festival closes
content:
The Nitjautik Music Festival opened and closed on a high note, as Lucy Johannes bookmarked the show with accordion tunes.


More than 100 people filled the community’s sports and leisure centre Friday and Saturday evening for the two-day festival, which

celebrated

 its fifth year.


Nitjautik is an Inuktitut term that refers to things that make sound, or music. In Nunavik, it’s also associated with the accordion, several members of the community explained.


Johannes, an accordion player from Kuujjuaq, learned to play the instrument by listening to her late father Tommy Johannes play music. At 18 years old she joined her father’s band, Kuujjuaq Band.


“I was so nervous,” she said, after a performance at Nitjautik. “I only close festivals, I don’t open.”


Qimutjuit, a band from Inukjuak, was also a crowd favourite, taking the stage to cheers and whistles.


Singer and guitarist Charlie Iqaluk, drummer Eric Atagotaaluk, keyboardist Paulosie Kasudluak and bassist Jobie Weetaluktuk have been playing together for more than 30 years.


The band played tunes from its debut self-titled album, including

 Sugavilli

 and

Inugama

, drawing children and elders toward the front of the stage to dance.


Other performers included Yaa, also known as Johnny Saunders, and his band; Ilagitt, a local Christian group; and Looee Arreak, an Inuktitut singer-songwriter from Nunavut.


The festival’s second night brought a mix of generations to the stage, including veteran Sugluk Band, which has roots that stretch back to the 1970s.


Later in the evening, with the clock nearing 11 p.m. and seats beginning to empty, The Trade Offs kept the remaining crowd moving.


In the end, Johannes got to close out the festival. She returned to the stage with her accordion, bringing the weekend full-circle.


But the crowd wasn’t ready to call it a night.


Davidee Angutinguak also returned after having performed earlier in the evening. He gave the crowd one more performance.


Billy Cain, president of the festival’s committee, said in an interview Sunday that organizers are expanding the festival next year.


“We are already planning for an extra night,” he said.


The festival began in 2021 after residents told Cain, who was mayor at the time, that they wanted a music festival in their community.


“It was a dream at first, and then it became a reality,” he said.


Yaa, aka Johnny Saunders, dedicates song “Lily-Anna” to his granddaughter during the Nitjautik Music Festival in Tasiujaq. (Photo by Dominique Gené)


Sugluk Band singer George Kakayuk performs with his grandson, Paulusie Kakayuk, Aug. 29 in Tasiujaq. (Photo by Dominique Gené)


Kathy Aputiarjuk takes the stage of Nitjautik Musical Festival in Tasiujaq on the second and final night. (Dominique Gené)


Peter Nassak rocks the Nitjautik stage in Tasiujaq as the festival nears its close. (Dominique Gené)

author: Eden Fineday
title: Help us keep the syilx Okanagan beat strong
content:
At the bottom of kɬúsx̌nítkʷ (Okanagan Lake) in snpink’tn (Penticton) on Aug. 26, community members gather and pray for the health of the land and for those affected by wildfires this summer. Photo by Aaron Hemens


This story was reprinted from our newsletter. Subscribe for updates

here

 and learn more about our Okanagan campaign

here

.


The Okanagan was the very first community IndigiNews committed to covering.


When we launched in 2020, we made a promise to report on syilx Okanagan communities week after week with a consistency that shows our care and respect for the peoples and their territories. 


For the past four years, that promise has been kept by our reporter in the region, Aaron Hemens.


Today, his work is at risk.


Aaron on the ground in April 2024, reporting on a cultural burn.


The funding that supported Aaron’s incredible reporting has ended. Without new support, IndigiNews will no longer be able to provide the same quality of dedicated storytelling we’ve offered in syilx Okanagan communities. 


Our goal

is to raise 

$35,000

 from our community of IndigiNews readers to keep Aaron covering the Okanagan. If we can reach our goal, we’ll be able to keep Aaron on the Okanagan beat for another full year — ensuring his vital reporting continues without interruption.


Keep the syilx Okanagan beat strong


We need to raise

$35,000

 to keep Aaron Hemens reporting from syilx Okanagan territory.


Help sustain independent, Indigenous-led local journalism.


Donate today


Aaron, a settler of mixed Filipino and European heritage, approaches his work with IndigiNews by centering the communities he’s reporting on. He believes journalism should be done in a good way — through building relationships that centre community protocol and accountability. 


As a man of colour, Aaron is very aware of what it means to be overlooked, misrepresented, and excluded in news media and beyond. This knowledge inspires him to show up at community gatherings, council meetings and court hearings to sensitively document the conversations that rarely make national headlines but nevertheless inform them.


nkwancinem Kim Montgomery dances at the Similkameen powwow arbour grounds on July 23, after being honoured for her 20 years of service with the Okanagan Nation Alliance. Photo by Aaron Hemens


This trust wasn’t built overnight. It took years of showing up for the people of the Okanagan. 


Across “Canada,” local journalism is disappearing. News deserts are spreading, hitting Indigenous communities particularly hard. As a result, important decisions are going undocumented, local histories are getting left unwritten, and people are less and less able to hold powerful institutions accountable. 


Stories disappear and, with them, access to the beating hearts of entire communities. 


At IndigiNews, we believe all communities deserve reporters who know the people they serve — not only during moments of crisis.


That’s why

we’re asking for your help

author: Giovanna DeStefanis
title: Women’s Equality Day: Many Gains, Still Work To Do
content:
On August 26, 1920, the 19th Amendment was certified, prohibiting the denial of the right to vote on the basis of sex. More than a century later, Women’s Equality Day commemorates that historic victory and the generations of suffragists who fought to secure it.

Women have won extraordinary gains in the 106 years since the 19th Amendment. But the right to vote was only one of the many rights women fought to secure. For much of US history, women were systematically excluded from political decision-making, denied equal access to education and employment, and treated as legally and economically dependent on men.

Through decades of organizing, litigation, and political action, feminists helped expand women’s access to education and the workplace, challenged sex discrimination, fought for protections against sexual harassment, and won greater economic independence, including the ability to obtain credit in their own names. Feminists also fought for access to contraception and abortion, recognizing that the ability to decide whether and when to have children is fundamental to women’s equality and autonomy.

Those struggles transformed the lives of generations of women. Today, women are outpacing men in college completion across every major racial and ethnic group in the US, while women are running for public office in record numbers. From the ballot box to the classroom, the workplace to the legislature, these gains did not happen by accident. They were won by generations of feminists who refused to accept inequality as inevitable. Even as women continue to break barriers and make historic progress, those hard-won gains are not guaranteed.

Yet Women’s Equality Day does not mean that women have achieved equality.

“I never thought that in the US we’d have people arguing to go back to the 19th century,” said Feminist Majority Foundation President and co-founder Eleanor Smeal. “It’s the 21st.”

Today, hard-won rights are once again under attack. The right to make decisions about our own bodies has been stripped away from millions of women since the Supreme Court overturned Roe. Across the country, abortion bans are forcing women to continue pregnancies against their will, while attacks on contraception and other reproductive health care threaten to further limit women’s control over their own lives. Taking that decision away is an attempt to take that power away as well.

Even the rights commemorated by Women’s Equality Day are being questioned. Some have openly advocated for restricting women’s voting for “household voting” that could give husbands greater control over how families vote. The fact that taking away women’s independent voting power is being discussed at all is a reminder that hard-won rights cannot be taken for granted.

“We never thought bad things would happen again,” said Kathy Spillar, executive director of Feminist Majority Foundation. “We demand equality, no less—but we must ensure that there is equality.”

That fight includes securing the Equal Right Amendment to explicitly prohibit discrimination on the basis of sex in the Constitution. Although the ERA has been fully ratified by the required 38 states, it has yet to be recognized as part of the Constitution. The majority of states have also adopted some form of constitutional protection for equal rights based on sex—or State ERA’s—but protections vary across the country.

Women’s Equality Day should be a celebration of how far women have come, but not a declaration of victory. We can celebrate the suffragists who fought for the ballot, the feminists who expanded women’s access to education and economic independence, and the generations of women who broke barriers in politics and public life. But equality is not guaranteed. We must continue fighting for reproductive freedom, an end to violence against women, equal opportunity and representation, and constitutional equality. Women’s Equality Day is a reminder of what feminists have won, and why we must keep fighting to protect it.
